pl-l4d4c7-d1e115.summary: Asks of what reality the baptism given to someone already just is a sacrament, and answers: of the reality that preceded, the remission already given through faith; of the remission of temporal penalty, or of sin committed meanwhile; and of the newness and cleanness given there. It is a sign of every reality of which it is the cause.
claims: Baptism of the justified signifies prior remission, remission of penalty, and newness.
A sacrament signifies all that it causes.

pl-l4d4c7-d1e118.summary: Notes that the reality sometimes precedes the sacrament and sometimes follows long after, as with those who approach insincerely and later repent: baptism then begins to profit them, being the sacrament of the sanctification they have by repenting.
claims: The reality of a sacrament can precede or follow it.
Baptism begins to profit the insincere when they repent.

pl-l4d4c7-d1e121.summary: Asks of what baptism would be the sacrament if they never repented or left their insincerity, and answers: of the reality that would have occurred if their enormity had not prevented it.
claims: Baptism without its reality signifies what it would have effected.

pl-l4d4c7-d1e125.summary: Raises the question whether infants receive grace in baptism by which, when they can use free choice, they may will and run. Adults who worthily receive the sacrament surely receive operating and cooperating grace, which they waste if they later sin mortally, losing the grace by the merit of sin; so they are said to insult the Holy Spirit and drive him away.
claims: Adults worthily baptized receive operating and cooperating grace.

pl-l4d4c7-d1e128.summary: States the question: whether infants, not yet using reason, receive in baptism grace by which they can will and do good when they come of age.

pl-l4d4c7-d1e131.summary: Argues that they seem not to: that grace is the charity and faith that prepare and help the will, and who would say they received faith and charity? But if they did not receive grace for good works as adults, the grace of baptism would not suffice for them in that state, and unless more were added they could not be good; and if it were not added, it would not be their fault, since they were justified from sin.
claims: It seems infants do not receive faith and charity in baptism.
If not, their baptismal grace would not suffice for adult goodness.

pl-l4d4c7-d1e144.summary: Reports the view of some that operating and cooperating grace is given to all infants in baptism as a gift, not in use, so that when they grow up they draw the use from the gift unless they extinguish it by sinning through free choice; so it is their fault, not a defect of grace, if they become bad.
claims: Some hold that infants receive grace in gift, not in use.
If baptized children become bad, it is their fault, not a defect of grace.

pl-l4d4c7.summary: Asks of what baptism given to one already just is the sacrament: of the remission already given through faith, of the remission of temporal penalty and any later sins, and of the newness and cleanness given there, since it signifies all it causes. The reality may precede the sacrament, or follow it, as with the insincere who later repent; if they never repent, it signifies what would have happened had their state not prevented it. Adults who receive worthily receive operating and cooperating grace, which they lose by mortal sin. Whether infants receive grace in baptism by which they can later will and do good is disputed: it seems not, since that grace is faith and charity; some hold they receive it as a gift, not in use, so that when they grow up they can use it unless they extinguish it by sin.
claims: Baptism given to the justified signifies prior remission, remission of penalty, and newness.
The reality may precede or follow the sacrament.
Adults worthily baptized receive operating and cooperating grace.
Some hold that infants receive grace in gift, not in use.
